Senses.Explanation: To roam at ease is to go or stay freely, without being tied or obstructed by what one meets. The Chan record uses it favorably but also polices the phrase against counterfeit freedom. Yongjue Yuanxian directly defines ‘what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely’ as remaining aloof and unattached amid every false scene, like a bird flying through the sky without the slightest tether and a dragon leaving the sea without the slightest obstruction (所謂逍遙放曠者，乃是於一切妄境，超然不著，如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). In the same address he denies that being tied by sounds, sights, wealth, or power can be called ranging freely and roaming at ease (豈曰放曠逍遙哉). Tianhuang Daowu tells Longtan Chongxin to roam at ease according to his nature, range freely following conditions, exhaust the ordinary mind, and retain no separate superior understanding (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). The Patriarchs' Hall Collection describes Danxia Tianran as delighting in clouds and waters and roaming at ease whether going or staying (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Tianyin Yuanxiu raises his staff and asks whether it is not roaming at ease and unbound; Shiyu Mingfang's community rule rejects taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease (將狂妄作逍遙者). An unnamed monk asks Lumen Fadeng about a person roaming at ease outside things, and Fadeng answers, ‘red and festering all over, unable to be supported’ (如何是逍遙物外底人；遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Yongjia Xuanjue's letter uses the ordinary motion frame ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷), which is not the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Juelang Daosheng's essay heading ‘Remarks on Free and Easy Wandering’ (提逍遙遊) names the longer title of a work by Zhuangzi; it is a family compound, not a fourth sense of the bare headword.
Senses.Note: Allowlisted concordance: 974 hits in 245 texts. Definition formulas yield three hits for ‘roaming-at-ease one(s)’, one direct ‘what is called roaming at ease’ formula, no exact hits for the other standard naming formulas, and seven ‘what is roaming at ease’ questions. Family counts include 53 hits for ‘roaming at ease and unbound’ (逍遙自在), 66 for ‘roam at ease according to one's nature’ (任性逍遙), nine for ‘range freely and roam at ease’ (放曠逍遙), 24 for ‘roaming at ease outside things’ (逍遙物外), and two for ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷). The 974-hit pool also contains the distinct personal title Master Xiaoyao, the place name Mount Xiaoyao, longer book-title language, and ordinary syntax; these were separated before the lexical depth count. Seven independent lexical witnesses remain after the longer-title family row is excluded. Favorable, critical, literal-motion, staff, instruction, narrative, and public-interview deployments all concern the same free-roaming action or state rather than different lexical things.

The Patriarchs' Hall Collection (祖堂集), in Danxia Tianran's biography, keeps Danxia as the grammatical subject across the full paragraph and describes Danxia Tianran delighting in clouds and waters and roaming at ease whether going or staying.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Record of Chan Master Juelang of Tianjie (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), authored by Juelang Daosheng, heads this essay ‘Remarks on Free and Easy Wandering’ and immediately names Zhuangzi. Senses.Explanation: Master Xiaoyao is the title by which the records preserve an otherwise unnamed successor of Jiashan Shanhui at Gao'an. This is a person, not the action of roaming at ease and not Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao. The Jingde Record places Xiaoyao Heshang on the Chan seat: Luxi states that thought after thought climbs after conditions while mind after mind is forever still; Xiaoyao says someone said that the previous evening, answers ‘I don't know,’ strikes Luxi across the mouth with the fly-whisk, and then addresses the assembly. The Patriarchs' Hall Collection independently says that Xiaoyao succeeded Jiashan and was at Gao'an, while acknowledging that it had not seen his conduct record and could not determine his beginning or end.
Senses.Note: The sources preserve no personal name beyond the title Xiaoyao Heshang. This source-attested title is kept exact pending the separate roster expansion. The person sense is distinguishable from the lexical and place senses from its target alone.

Senses.Explanation: Mount Xiaoyao is the Jiangxi monastery mountain attached in lineage headings to Xiaoyao Huaizhong, a successor of Jiashan Shanhui. Two independent compilations use the full heading ‘Chan Master Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao in Jiangxi’ (江西逍遙山懷忠禪師). The mountain is a place, not Master Xiaoyao and not the act of roaming through terrain.
Senses.Note: The sources preserve Huaizhong's personal name and Mount Xiaoyao location. The title Xiaoyao Heshang belongs to a different successor of Jiashan at Gao'an. The separately anchored lexical phrase ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ remains verb-plus-object syntax under the first sense rather than evidence for this place.
